evidence: Cato Agr. 28.1: bene cum rādīcibus eximitō
terms.comment: Mostly in the plural for a plant’s roots: rādīcēs agere or capere, “to take root” (Varro, Cato), ab rādīcibus, “by the roots” (Caesar). Also the root of the tongue or of a hair, the foot of a mountain (sub rādīce montis, Cato Agr. 1.3), and an edible root, especially the radish (Lewis & Short). The root of a matter is fōns or orīgō (see source).

terms.gloss: the stock: the lower trunk with its roots
evidence: Liv. 21.36.1: virgulta ac stirpēs circā ēminentēs
terms.comment: The base of a plant, roots and all, and so a young plant or shrub; figuratively a family’s stock or lineage (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: cum serēs, bene cum rādīcibus eximitō cum terrā suā quam plūrimā circumligātōque, utī ferre possīs
phrases.english: when you transplant it, lift it out well with its roots and as much of its own soil as you can, and tie it round so that you can carry it

phrases.latin: vēra glōria rādīcēs agit atque etiam prōpāgātur, ficta omnia celeriter tamquam flōsculī dēcidunt
phrases.english: true glory puts down roots and even spreads; everything false quickly drops, like little blossoms

phrases.latin: trūditur ē siccō rādīx oleāgina lignō
phrases.english: an olive root pushes out of the dry wood
